place-work.text: A drinking cup’s named owner and proposed courtly use differ from an excavated household’s provisioning evidence. Ceramic work, patronage and exchange can be compared across these contexts without turning a regional attribution into a findspot or assigning this cup a maker from another object.

participation.text: An elite owner’s name and imagery connect rank with food and fertility; other voices are less directly represented.

evidence.text: The proposed regional origin rests on comparisons rather than a documented excavation of this vessel.

name: A Maya drinking vessel: text, food and rank
geographicPrecision: Broad hypothesized region; no precise excavated findspot is claimed.

interval.label: Seventh–eighth centuries CE
interval.note: Catalogue object range; not a lifespan for Maya peoples, who continue today.

question: What can a name on a cup tell us—and what does it leave open?
summary: A made container joined food, imagery and a named owner. Its courtly interpretation becomes more useful beside evidence for ceramic making, attributed painters and household provisioning elsewhere. Each source keeps its own date, place and limits.

sections.title: A container joined several kinds of work
sections.text: This large ceramic cup brings making and representation together. Fine incised outlines run across its pale surface, while the catalogue proposes a painted-stucco finish near the rim. Doyle’s wider account describes Maya potters forming vessels by hand and choosing clay, additives and surfaces before firing. Such choices made containers durable and gave artists a working surface. They supply a production context for this cup, while its particular clay recipe, workshop and maker remain unrecorded.

citations.locator: Artwork Details; Description: incisions and rim ornamentation; existing photograph

sections.title: Naming a relationship
sections.text: The museum reads the short text as identifying a drinking cup belonging to Baje(?) Kaan, or Chan, Took’, a ruler or noble. Part of that reading remains uncertain. It makes ownership a visible social relationship: a named person could be connected with a container used for serving and display. The figure and signs also share the same composition. The catalogue considers it possible that the seated figure represents the named owner; the text supplies no polity.

citations.locator: Description: ownership text; text-image relationship; polity paragraph

sections.title: Food, display and exchange
sections.text: Doyle relates the cup’s form to cacao preparation scenes on other vessels, where pouring makes froth. Shared dipping is a proposed reconstruction of use. The museum reads imagery of agricultural fertility as connecting the represented ruler with food and renewal. In the wider Classic-period account, finely made vessels also served as diplomatic gifts between courts and governors. Their circulation could carry skilled work and messages about relationships, without establishing a particular gift event for this cup.

citations.locator: Cacao preparation and presumable shared dipping

sections.title: Makers and patrons can enter the record
sections.text: Some other vessels allow the maker-patron relationship to be studied more closely. Princeton’s account attributes an Ik’ dish around 755 CE to Mo?-n Buluch Laj and names Yajawte’ K’ihnich as patron. It also describes signed cups from that courtly setting. These records make skilled people visible beside their patrons. They do not supply a maker for the selected vessel or prove that its owner made it.

sections.title: Other households produced and exchanged
sections.text: A separate excavated village, Cerén in present-day El Salvador, brings households into view. Sheets describes people producing food and goods for their own use, making surplus through part-time specialties and exchanging products with neighbors or at elite centers. Groundstone tools, painted gourds and plant fibers enter that account. A later botanical study documents productive gardens and outfields. This evidence explains daily work beyond courtly imagery; it does not locate this museum cup at Cerén.

deeperReading.title: An argued origin is different from a findspot
deeperReading.text: The Tabasco association rests on comparisons in the museum’s account: a similar name on a Comalcalco brick and incised cylinders described from Jonuta. The original brick edition and Berlin study were not consulted here. The cup’s appearance in Europe in 1961 and a Swiss collection notice in 1964 belong to its modern documentary history. Those notices neither record its excavation nor establish a complete ancient itinerary. The current provenance-tab text was not exposed.

citations.locator: Description: Comalcalco/Jonuta hypothesis and 1961/1964 publication history

deeperReading.title: Ownership, contents and making ask different questions
deeperReading.text: Doyle explains that texts on other vessels can name their type, contents, owner or giver. This cup’s short ownership statement does not provide all those answers. An artist signature would address another relationship again. Distinguishing these statements keeps the named owner from becoming an invented maker and the broader cacao interpretation from becoming a translation of a word absent from the supplied ownership reading.

deeperReading.title: Preservation shapes the household comparison
deeperReading.text: Cerén’s volcanic burial preserved domestic contexts unusually well. UNESCO’s Description uses approximately 600 CE, while the 2020 research abstract uses approximately 660 CE. These conventions remain attributed. The consulted research abstracts support a bounded household comparison, rather than a complete reconstruction of every residence or all Maya economies. A decorated courtly object and a preserved village make different work visible.

evidenceReading.title: Ownership, contents and household context
evidenceReading.introduction: These supplied passages paraphrase the consulted sources. Visible outlines, a museum decipherment, a use interpretation and an excavated household comparison support different claims.

items.label: A deciphered ownership relationship
items.text: The museum reads a named person’s drinking cup, with part of the name uncertain, and says the inscription gives no polity. It considers the pictured figure possibly the owner.
items.interpretation: The photograph supplies incised forms; the ownership reading depends on the museum’s epigraphic interpretation. Keep Baje(?) and Kaan/Chan alternatives. A named owner does not identify the maker or establish a complete court scene.

items.text: Doyle compares the vessel form with cacao preparation depicted on other cups, and describes shared dipping as presumable. The selected short ownership phrase does not itself identify cacao.
items.interpretation: This is a curatorial interpretation connecting form, imagery and other scenes. No residue assay for this specimen was consulted. Do not turn a reconstructed serving practice into an observed event or copy the separately copyrighted rollout/drawings.

items.label: Households supplied goods through several domains
items.text: Sheets’s Cerén abstract distinguishes production for household use, part-time surplus exchange with other households and acquisition of some goods through elite centers. The 2020 botanical abstract describes gardens and outfields.
items.interpretation: These are source-qualified findings from a separately excavated village. They extend the inquiry to provisioning and exchange without locating this cup there or making all Maya households alike. Only exposed abstracts/selected first-page text were read.

familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the museum reads this as a named person’s drinking cup, with part of the name uncertain, and says the text gives no polity. It interprets cacao use through comparisons. At separately excavated Cerén, households produced food and goods and exchanged some products; those finds do not locate this cup. Incised outlines can be observed, while ownership requires decipherment and contents require interpretation. A maker, exact findspot and every household’s menu remain unestablished.

review.reviewer: Codex selected primary/institutional source consultation and internal author review; not independent historian, epigrapher or community approval
review.scope: Selected ceramic, food and ownership account, separately sourced courts and households, three evidence readings, supplied family capsule, attributed reference phases and modern photograph observations. The entire original case interval, identity, claims, object IDs/order, image bytes and prior dimensions remain intact. The Cerén location is a separately sourced household comparison.
limitations: The Met catalogue and 2014/2017 museum texts are attributed interpretations. No new decipherment, named polity, maker, secure excavated origin, residue assay, measured ceramic recipe or workshop identified for 1992.4. The Comalcalco brick edition, Berlin paper, Kerr database and original epigraphic technical works were not consulted.

Current complete provenance-tab text, conservation history, photograph creation date and remote-byte parity were not exposed or verified. Earlier 26 October source scope is retained rather than presented as comprehensively renewed. 1961/1964 documentation and 1992 acquisition belong outside ancient reference phases.

Sheets 2000 was read at exposed abstract/metadata scope. Slotten/Lentz/Sheets 2020 was read through the primary PDF search-index abstract/first-page Introduction and rights footer; full PDF exceeded tool size, publisher 403 and eScholarship 429 were not bypassed. No full methods/results, figures, inventories or original calibration consulted.

UNESCO c. 600 and 2020 abstract c. 660 conventions remain attributed; the first-page reported 592–660 interval is not a new calibration. Cerén is a separate comparison and a modern UNESCO reference point, never this cup’s findspot, route or a universal Maya household. Named/attributed Ik’ painter and patron belong to a different object and place.

The existing collection photograph is eligible public-domain/CC0 imagery; the ©Justin Kerr rollout and separately credited article drawings are excluded. Modern observation markers are a separate editorial layer with their own credit, date and licence. They preserve the underlying photograph and do not supply a new decipherment, pigment analysis or reconstruction.
Independent historian/epigrapher/community review, real family use, human screen-reader behavior, physical devices and physical print quality remain open.

placeStudy.description: The single point is a modern UNESCO site reference in El Salvador, rounded to 0.001 degree. It locates the excavated household comparison, never the cup’s origin or a direct journey from its proposed Tabasco association. The original broad cup locator remains unchanged. The schematic modern coastline supplies orientation, not an ancient shoreline.
